questions.prompt: What is the 'transparency of experience', as Harman (1990) describes it?

options.text: When attending to an experience, one finds only features of the object presented, not intrinsic features of the experience
Experiences are fully available to introspection without error
options.why_wrong: Transparency is not a claim of infallibility.

options.text: Brain states are visible in imaging
options.why_wrong: This is not the philosophical notion.

options.text: Experience reveals the physical nature of its own vehicle
options.why_wrong: Transparency says the vehicle is not revealed.

questions.explanation: Attending to your experience of a tree, you find only the tree as presented. Representationalists take this to support the view that phenomenal character is fixed by what an experience represents.

sources.citation: Harman, G. (1990). The intrinsic quality of experience. Philosophical Perspectives 4, 31-52.
Tye, M. (1995). Ten Problems of Consciousness: A Representational Theory of the Phenomenal Mind. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of higher-order theory and proponent is correct?

options.text: Higher-order thought: Armstrong; higher-order perception: Rosenthal
Higher-order thought: Rosenthal; higher-order perception (inner sense): Armstrong and Lycan
Higher-order thought: Block; higher-order perception: Dennett
options.why_wrong: Block is a prominent critic of higher-order theories.

options.text: Higher-order thought: Harman; higher-order perception: Tye
options.why_wrong: Harman and Tye are representationalists about first-order experience.

questions.explanation: Rosenthal holds that a state is conscious when one has a suitable thought that one is in it. Armstrong and Lycan model the higher-order state as an inner perception or monitoring, in the line of Locke's 'inner sense'.

sources.citation: Rosenthal, D. M. (2005). Consciousness and Mind. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
Armstrong, D. M. (1968). A Materialist Theory of the Mind. London: Routledge and Kegan Paul.
Lycan, W. G. (1996). Consciousness and Experience. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.

questions.prompt: What is the misrepresentation objection to higher-order theories?

options.text: Higher-order states are too slow to explain conscious timing

options.why_wrong: They are often said to handle blindsight well.

options.text: If a higher-order state can represent a first-order state that does not exist, it is unclear what is conscious

options.why_wrong: That is a separate objection, about overintellectualising.

questions.explanation: A higher-order representation might target a state that is absent or different. Block argues this makes the theory incoherent; Rosenthal replies that the conscious state is the one the higher-order state represents one as being in.

sources.citation: Block, N. (2011). The higher order approach to consciousness is defunct. Analysis 71(3), 419-431.
Rosenthal, D. M. (2011). Exaggerated reports: reply to Block. Analysis 71(3), 431-437.
